text:
Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Shea v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 ABQB 241

Date:
20220405

Docket:
2103 10019

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Shawn Shea

Applicant

- and -

Attorney General of Canada and Warden of Bowden Institution - Lawrence Hartigan and Warden of Edmonton Institution

Respondents

_______________________________________________________

Memorandum of Decision

of the

Honourable Madam Justice

M. Hayes-Richards

_______________________________________________________

I.          Introduction

[
1
]

Shawn Shea [Mr. Shea] is a dangerous offender who is serving an indeterminate sentence in Correctional Service of Canada [CSC] facilities. On November 10, 2021, Mr. Shea filed an “Application for Habeas Corpus with certiorari in aid thereof” that named the Attorney General of Canada, the Warden of Bowden Institution, Lawrence Hartigan, and the Warden of the Edmonton Institution as Respondents [Application]. Mr. Shea has self-represented throughout this proceeding.

[
2
]

The body of the Application reads:

Basis for this claim:

1.         Violations of the CCRR s sec 39 to 44 and Charter violations sec 7 9

2.         Appeal offender accuracy level Dec # 51

3.         Appealing Institutional Transfer to Edmonton Max Torture Dec # 51

Remedy Sought:

2.         Release back to open population at a Medium Security Federal Institution

3.         Reimbursed For Lost Liberty,

4.         Reimbursement for lost earnings from Loss of beadwork, leatherwork and drawing art work Profits.

Affidavit or other evidence to be used in support of this application

4.         The secret segregation, quarantine, short staff.

5.         Affidavit of Shawn SHEA dated: 2021-06-01

6.         Correctional Service of Canada Institutional reports that are currently in possession of the ‘Service’

7.         Video recordings Audio (From Jan 2015 to Present) Range micro phones. Wire taps.

8.         Observations Reports from Jan 2015 till Present.

9.         Testimony of Inmates and Institution Staff.

10.       The wire taps of the Phone calls S.I.O. At Saskatewuan Penitentiary new of allege hit on my life, Learned on 2020-06-29 and was obligated to inform and protect me.

11.       CCCR sec 24

12.       Complaints, Rebuttals, Grievances

13.       Full and complete disclosure as per Regina. v.
Stinchcombe

14.
Security Intelligence Officer Reports and Sources Reliability Tests between 2015 and present

15.
All staff Reports.

[Sic, emphasis in original.]

[
3
]

Mr. Shea’s Application was accompanied by Affidavits of Mr. Shea, sworn on March 25, 2021 and May 31, 2021, and other items, including:

1.         communications and complaint process documents prepared by Mr. Shea and CSC staff,

2.         a “Brief” (written rebuttal) to the decision that Mr. Shea should be transferred from the Bowden Institution (medium security) to the Edmonton Institution (maximum security) in 2021, and

3.         newspaper clippings.

[
4
]

Together, these materials make the following claims:

1.         On March 12, 2021, a conflict occurred between Mr. Shea and a CSC officer in the Bowden Institution. Mr. Shea says there was no legitimate basis for this conflict, which was the CSC officer’s fault. That officer is a sexual deviant and engaged in “perverted behaviour.” That confrontation led to Mr. Shea being improperly reclassified and transferred to the Edmonton Institution.

2.         The transfer relied on inaccurate information about Mr. Shea and his conduct, including Mr. Shea had received contraband via a “drone drop”, Mr. Shea is involved in Bowden Institution drug trafficking, and that Mr. Shea was found with “a shank” (an ersatz stabbing weapon).

3.         Mr. Shea says the Warden of the Bowden Institution improperly transferred Mr. Shea because Mr. Shea was never criminally charged for his alleged misconduct, Mr. Shea was denied access to video recordings, and, globally, the evidence did not support Mr. Shea’s transfer. Mr. Shea calls his transfer procedurally unfair.

4.         Mr. Shea complains about the conditions in the Edmonton Institution, which he says are “torture” and the product of systematic corruption. Mr. Shea’s complaints are at least in part about conditions and procedures that resulted from COVID-19 management steps in the Edmonton Institution. Mr. Shea also points to what he says is a problematic culture in the Edmonton Institution.

5.         Mr. Shea alleges he has been improperly denied access to computers, the Internet, and case law. He complains that programming and activities at the Edmonton Institution are inadequate.

[
5
]

Steps Mr. Shea seeks in his written materials include:

1.         “send back to Medium”,

2.         consultation and collaboration with Edmonton Institution staff concerning conditions in that institution, and how to improve those conditions,

3.         “find staff to work”,

4.         a “Wii Fit” system,

5.         $5,000 for lost wages, legal fees, expenses, and time,

6.         access to computers, the Internet, legal resources, programs, and applications,

7.         his “Legal Assistant” is present at hearings, and

8.         correction of inaccurate information “used against me.”

[
6
]

Mr. Shea’s Application was first addressed in Queen’s Bench Appearance Court on December 10, 2021. At that point Justice Richardson set deadlines for filing with the Court of the certified record, argument and affidavit evidence by Justice Canada, and reply submissions by Mr. Shea. Oral argument was set for February 23, 2022.

II.        The February 23, 2022 Hearing and Party Submissions

[
7
]

An issue emerged during the February 23, 2022 hearing. Justice Canada acts on behalf of the Respondents. It came to light that Justice Canada had not received much of the material that the Court had received from Mr. Shea on November 10, 2021. As a consequence, the party’s submissions were divided. Mr. Shea made oral submissions on February 23, 2022. Justice Canada had filed a Written Representation on February 11, 2022, and made further oral submission at the February 23, 2022 hearing. After review of the materials from Mr. Shea that Justice Canada had not previously received, Justice Canada provided Supplemental Written Representations on March 10, 2022.

[
8
]

Mr. Shea at the February 23, 2022 hearing agreed that, if he had any further submissions or responses to make to Justice Canada’s March 10, 2022 argument, that Mr. Shea would supply those to the Court as of March 14, 2022. No further documents have been received by Mr. Shea, post-March 10, 2022.

[
9
]

I will review and summarize each parties’ submissions as a whole, rather than according to the incremental manner in which the submissions were received.

A.        Mr. Shea

[
10
]

At the February 23, 2022 hearing, Mr. Shea’s explained that his Application had several aspects. One was his transfer to the Edmonton Institution. Mr. Shea reviewed his complaints concerning the factual basis for his transfer. Mr. Shea did acknowledge his conflict with the Bowden Institution guard that triggered his transfer. He admitted that he had argued with that guard. However, Mr. Shea alleged what followed was disproportionate, it was a “little incident” that ultimately was triggered by Mr. Shea’s addiction to cigarettes. The outcome was “disproportionate” and “inhumane”; all Mr. Shea did is call the CSC officer “a pervert” and “a bitch”; there was no threat. If there was a problem between Mr. Shea and the guard, that should have been addressed by informal conflict resolution processes. Mr. Shea says he has a good institutional record. Mr. Shea reports his Parole Officer called Mr. Shea “the Nelson Mandela of Canada.”

[
11
]

Mr. Shea expanded on other reasons he concludes that the transfer decision was unfair and improper. Mr. Shea says no transfer should occur, except with the formal hearing that Mr. Shea had demanded. Mr. Shea’s position is that unless he was criminally charged and convicted of drug offenses, then any evidence of that is excluded. Furthermore, any drug-related evidence should be rejected because CSC employees contaminate objects, documents, and mail with drugs.

[
12
]

The Warden was “judge, jury, and executioner”. Poor people and indigenous people, like Mr. Shea, cannot get justice. Mr. Shea explained he is a persecuted dangerous offender, who just found out he is 2% Indigenous. Mr. Shea also complained he was not allowed to have a “legal assistant”, who is Jewish, participate in his transfer arguments, because of a timing conflict with Passover. In Mr. Shea’s written materials this appears to be “Mitch Nome”. Mr. Shea confirmed Mr. Nome was not a lawyer, but a fellow inmate. I note Mr. Shea’s written materials also indicate his formal written rebuttal in response to his transfer from the Bowden Institution to Edmonton Institution was prepared after consultation with, and the assistance of, a lawyer: “Amanda Hart”.

[
13
]

However, at Mr. Shea’s hearing before me, he indicated he no longer cares about his transfer from Bowden Institution to the Edmonton Institution. He wanted to talk about the Edmonton Institution: “the worst jail in Canada”. Mr. Shea argued there is sexual abuse at the Edmonton Institution. He called that facility “a modern-day residential school”, worse than Afghanistan, corrupt, and reported an inmate was shot with a machine gun. He says inmates are double doored so its like “Fight Club”, that he is in jail because the guards set up a fight, and that inmates are held in “secret segregation”.

B.        The Respondents

[
14
]

The Respondents take the position that the only valid subject for
habeas corpus
review is the transfer of Mr. Shea from the Bowden Institution to the Edmonton Institution. That satisfies the criteria for a justiciable
habeas corpus
application, since Mr. Shea has:

1.         identified, and the Respondents acknowledge, that Mr. Shea has experienced a reduction in his residual liberty when he was transferred from a medium security to a maximum security facility;

2.         alleged that the transfer decision was illegal for a number of reasons, including that the decision to transfer was disproportionate, based on incorrect facts, and unreasonable.

[
15
]

Counsel for the Respondents reviewed evidence from 2020 onward that Mr. Shea was involved in drug trafficking into the Bowden Institution, possessed shanks, and was acting in an unusual and aggressive manner on March 12, 2021 that implied drug use. Other relevant information was that monitored telephone communications between Mr. Shea and his wife was evidence of money transfers that corresponded with Mr. Shea’s institutional drug trafficking. Mr. Shea was the ringleader for the Bowden Institutional drug trafficking network. That was a contributing reason for Mr. Shea’s transfer to the Edmonton Institution. He could not be effectively managed in Bowden Institution. Mr. Shea is also facing charges on this basis.

[
16
]

The Respondents’ position is that the Bowden Institution Warden followed procedure. The Warden received, considered, and responded to Mr. Shea’s rebuttal in the final reasons for Mr. Shea’s transfer. Processes set in the
Corrections and Conditional Release Act
, SC 1992, c 20 [
CCRA
] and
Corrections and Conditional Release Regulations
, SOR/92-620 [
CCRR
] were followed. The resulting decision is based on fact, reasonable, and procedurally fair.

[
17
]

As for Mr. Shea’s complaints concerning the Edmonton Institution and conditions there, the Respondents conclude the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench has no
habeas corpus
authority to evaluate Mr. Shea’s complaints. Instead, allegations of improper prison conditions, programming, and access to technology are properly subjects for the
CCRA
and
CCRR
complaints process, followed potentially by judicial review before the Federal Courts. Furthermore, allegations about the Edmonton Institution and other related information is inadmissible and/or irrelevant since claims by Mr. Shea about the Edmonton Institution are not part of the record concerning Mr. Shea’s transfer. Globally, Mr. Shea’s written materials are not a proper affidavit, and most allegations and claims were inadequately particularized, or simply bald allegations.

[
18
]

The Respondents position is the decision to transfer Mr. Shea was procedurally fair, and compliant with the
CCRA
and
CCRR
. Certain information was properly withheld from Mr. Shea pursuant to
CCRA
s 27(3) for valid security and safety reasons. That said, Mr. Shea received a summary, or “gist”, of that information and its sources that was an adequate basis for Mr. Shea to make a full and substantive response. The Respondents provided a “sealed affidavit” to the Court that describes the
CCRA
s 27(3) evidence in full.

[
19
]

The Respondents stress this Court’s review of the decision to transfer Mr. Shea is conducted on a reasonableness standard:
Mission Institution v Khela
,
2014 SCC 24
. A reasonable decision must be rational and logical, internally coherent and justified by the facts and law:
Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov
,
2019 SCC 65
. CSC officials have special expertise and knowledge that is due deference, particularly when evaluating inmate risk and institutional safety:
Mission Institution v Khela
.

[
20
]

The reasons to transfer Mr. Shea satisfy those criteria. The Warden considered and responded to Mr. Shea’s rebuttal, and applied the factors identified in
CCRR
s 17. That was based on the facts concerning Mr. Shea and his problematic conduct.

[
21
]

The Respondents ask the Court to affirm that Mr. Shea’s transfer was lawful and reasonable, dismiss Mr. Shea’s
habeas corpus
application, and award costs of $250.

III.       Analysis

A.        Preliminary Issue - Conditions at the Edmonton Institution, and Impossible Remedies

[
22
]

As a preliminary step, I reject Mr. Shea’s complaints concerning his conditions at the Edmonton Institution. The law in Canada is clear that, for incarcerated persons,
habeas corpus
may be available to a serving prisoner where the incarcerated person is placed into a “new detention” under a “legal authority” that results in a “distinct form of confinement or detention” which is “a significant reduction in the residual liberty of the inmate”:
R v Miller
,
1985 CanLII 22 (SCC)
, [1985] 2 SCR 613 at 640-641;
May v Ferndale Institution
,
2005 SCC 82
at paras
27-28
; and
Gogan v Attorney General of Canada
,
2017 ABQB 609
at paras
41-52
. The transfer of Mr. Shea from the Bowden Institution to the Edmonton Institution satisfies those criteria.

[
23
]

However, the issues that Mr. Shea identifies with the Edmonton Institution do not fall into the
habeas corpus
jurisdiction. For example:

•

Trivial, intermittent, and transient losses of residual liberty do not attract
Charter
or
habeas corpus
review:
Dumas v Leclerc Institute
,
1986 CanLII 38 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 SCR 459 at para
10
, 34 DLR (4th) 427;
R v Gamble
,
1988 CanLII 15 (SCC)
, [1988] 2 SCR 595 at 637, 45 CCC (3d) 204;
Cunningham v Canada
,
1993 CanLII 139 (SCC)
, [1993] 2 SCR 143 at 151, 20 CR (4th) 57;
Canada (Attorney General) v Whaling
,
2014 SCC 20
at paras
57-58
, [2014] 1 SCR 392;
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
,
2017 ABQB 237
at para
39-41
, 54 Alta LR (6th) 135, appeal abandoned, Edmonton 1603-0287AC (Alta CA).

•

Habeas corpus
provides no remedy where an incarcerated person complains about a loss of privileges:
R v Miller
, at para
35
;
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
, at para
25
.

•

Denial or inability to access rehabilitative programming is not a basis for
habeas corpus
:
Cunningham v Canada
; see also
Canada (Attorney General) v Whaling
, at para
57
;
Lord v Coulter
,
2007 BCSC 1758
at para
60
, 72 Admin LR (4th) 264, affirmed
2009 BCCA 62
at para
5
, 266 BCAC 122;
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
at para
28
.

•

Habeas corpus
is not a remedy for claims of inadequate legal services, access to computers, and legal resources:
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
at paras
60-68
;
Lee v Canada (Attorney General)
,
2018 ABQB 40
at para
40
.

[
24
]

Furthermore, Mr. Shea has sought remedies that are not available via
habeas corpus
, such as lost wages, and a “Wii Fit” system.
Habeas corpus
has one powerful but specialized function: 1) to test whether a detention is or is not lawful, and 2) if that detention is not lawful, to order release:
Charter
s 10(c);
Mission Institution v Khela
at para
30
. The only remedy that may result from a
habeas corpus
application is release:
Charter
s 10(c);
Mission Institution v Khela
at paras
27-30
. Slatter JA recently stressed in
R v Latham
,
2018 ABCA 308
at para
7
, leave to SCC refused, 38437 (14 March 2019) that
habeas corpus
is not “... some sort of legal Swiss Army knife that can be used to engage any grievance ... Habeas corpus is a limited remedy designed to address wrongful detentions and loss of liberty only.”

[
25
]

This Court’s jurisdiction in relation to CSC facilities, their operations, and inmates, is extremely limited.
Federal Courts Act
, RSC 1985, c F-7, s 18(1) gives the Federal Courts
exclusive
jurisdiction to issue a writ of
certiorari
in relation to federal boards, commissions, or other tribunals. In
Mission Institution v Khela
at paras
31-32
, Lebel J is explicit that any “decisions made within federal prison walls” are the
sole domain
of the Federal Courts - including “writs of certiorari” - except for
habeas corpus
which is omitted from the relevant
Federal Courts Act
provisions.

[
26
]

For these reasons I dismiss Mr. Shea’s complaints concerning conditions at the Edmonton Institution, and his seeking remedies other than release to his pre-transfer conditions. This Court has no
habeas corpus
jurisdiction to respond to these alleged issues.

B.        Transfer From Bowden Institution to Edmonton Institution

[
27
]

That leaves the question of the legality of Mr. Shea’s transfer from the Bowden Institution to the Edmonton Institution. The parties agree, and I accept, that Mr. Shea has satisfied the
Mission Institution v Khela
threshold criteria that 1) Mr. Shea prove a deprivation of residual liberty on a balance of probabilities, and 2) allege the decision to transfer Mr. Shea was potentially illegal. That reverses the onus on the parties:
Mission Institution v Khela
at para
30
. The next step is to determine whether Counsel for Justice Canada have established, on a balance of probabilities, that the transfer decision was legal.

1.         Evidence Issues and the Sealed Affidavit

[
28
]

One of the reasons that Mr. Shea advanced as to why his transfer was illegal is that, factually, there was no basis for it. Mr. Shea’s argument, as I understand it, has two basic points: 1) the March 12, 2021 confrontation with the Bowden Institution CSC officer does not establish wrongdoing by Mr. Shea - it was the guard’s fault, and 2) the evidence does not support Mr. Shea was engaged in other misconduct including trafficking and drug use, and possessing contraband, such as shanks.

[
29
]

I reject Mr. Shea’s argument. I have carefully reviewed the Certified Record, and the sealed affidavit provided by the Respondents. First, I conclude that the Warden of Bowden Institution was correct to withhold the sealed affidavit information from Mr. Shea, pursuant to
CCRA
s 27(3). Second, I find as fact that the “gist” provided in the CSC decisions of the contents of the sealed affidavit was accurate, and sufficient to provide Mr. Shea with the opportunity to make an effective, informed, and meaningful response to the allegations against him.

[
30
]

Third, I conclude that the Respondents are correct. The evidence available to the Warden was not only a reasonable basis to order Mr. Shea’s transfer, but, factually, that Mr. Shea did engage in the alleged misconduct. In short, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that there was an adequate factual foundation for the decision to transfer Mr. Shea to a maximum security facility.

2.         Procedure Unfairness

[
31
]

Mr. Shea makes a number of open-ended allegations that the procedure followed in the decision to transfer him was illegal. For example, Mr. Shea demands a hearing to decide whether he should have been transferred. Where those allegations by Mr. Shea run contrary to the procedure in the
CCRA
and
CCRR
, I conclude Mr. Shea has no basis for those complaints. CSC officials were simply following the procedure set for them by Parliament.

[
32
]

The other procedural issue Mr. Shea has advanced is that the transfer decision procedure was unfair because Mr. Shea’s “legal assistant” “Mitch Nome” was not available due to religious commitments. Courts have recognized a right of inmates to a reasonable opportunity to consult and retain counsel (
Williams v Canada (Correctional Services)
,
[1993] 1 FC 710, 149 NR 140 (FCA)
;
Shoemaker v Canada (Drumheller Institution)
,
2018 ABQB 851
at paras
58-59
). That is codified in
CCRR
s 97(2). I conclude that the Respondents are correct that no parallel right exists for non-lawyer “legal assistants”.

[
33
]

In any case, Mr. Shea’s Written Rebuttal to the transfer decision that was a part of Mr. Shea’s November 10, 2021 materials and the certified record is explicit: Mr. Shea conducted “extensive consultations” and obtained assistance from his legal counsel, Amanda Hart, in preparing Mr. Shea’s response to the Bowden Institution Warden’s decision that Mr. Shea should be transferred to a higher security detention facility. The absence of Mr. Shea’s “legal assistant” is irrelevant since Mr. Shea had access to and had “... extensive consultations with my
legal counsel - Amanda HART
over the past
x2
weeks ...” [emphasis in original].

[
34
]

I, therefore, conclude Counsel for the Respondents have rebutted, on a balance of probabilities, Mr. Shea’s allegation that the decision to transfer him to the Edmonton Institution was procedurally unfair.

3.         Unreasonable Decision

[
35
]

I accept Counsel for the Respondents’ summary and review of the relevant law for the standard of review and legal principles that I should apply when I evaluate the Warden of the Bowden Institution’s reasons to transfer Mr. Shea to the Edmonton Institution via
habeas corpus
. After careful review of the certified record, and, in particular:

1.         the March 16, 2021 Assessment for Decision, Inst. Transfer (Involuntary),

2.         the March 18, 2021 Notice of Involuntary Transfer/Movement Recommendation,

3.         the March 25, 2021 Addendum to Assessment for Decision,

4.         the March 29, 2021 Referral Decision Sheet for Inst. Transfer (Involuntary), and

5.         the March 29, 2021 Referral Decision Sheet for Offender Security Level.

[
36
]

I find as fact and law, and on a balance of probabilities, that the Warden’s decisions to reclassify and transfer Mr. Shea were reasonable and procedurally fair. I note that Mr. Shea’s rebuttal was chiefly that he disclaimed any involvement in institutional drug culture and possession of contraband, despite physical and electronic evidence to the contrary. The Warden’s conclusions based on the available evidence were reasonable, transparent, internally consistent, logical, and responded in substance to Mr. Shea’s written rebuttal.

[
37
]

As I have concluded, the Warden was correct to refuse Mr. Shea’s demand for assistance from his “legal assistant” “Mitch Nome”, since Mr. Shea had instead had access to, and factually consulted with, an actual lawyer. The decision reviewed and documented Mr. Shea’s record, and considered the issues relevant to Mr. Shea’s transfer, such as his threat and misconduct indicia, and other related questions, such as potential incompatible inmates in the Edmonton Institution. The result was a balanced and reasoned decision. I not only conclude that the Warden’s decision was reasonable, but also correct. Mr. Shea should have been transferred to a higher security CSC facility, and the Edmonton Institution was an appropriate alternative.

[
38
]

Given these determinations, I find that the Respondents have rebutted Mr. Shea’s allegation that the decision to transfer Mr. Shea to the Edmonton Institution was unreasonable.

IV.       Conclusion

[
39
]

Mr. Shea’s
habeas corpus
application is dismissed. Following this Court’s usual practice (
Loughlin v Her Majesty the Queen
,
2018 ABQB 45
), Mr. Shea is ordered to pay costs. The amount sought by the Respondents, $250, is reasonable. I order Mr. Shea make that payment, forthwith.

[
40
]

Counsel for the Respondents shall prepare the order giving effect to this Decision. Mr. Shea’s
approval of the Order is not required, pursuant to
Rule
9.4(2)(c)
.

Heard on the
23
rd
day of February, 2022.

Dated
at the City of Edmonton, Alberta this
5
th
day of April, 2022.

M. Hayes-Richards

J.C.Q.B.A.

Appearances:

Shawn Shea

for the Self-Represented Litigant

Keelan Sinnott and Duncan McManus

Department of Justice Canada

Prairie Region

for the Respondents
